_comment: Canonical character and system voice lines for the game. Narration is excluded because it is audiobook-only. `audio` points at the same clip the audiobook plays: one generated line, used in both places.

lines.text: Warning. Unauthorized system access.
What? Okay, I'm awake.
That's not good.
Come on. What are you doing?
No. Where'd you go?
Security protocol violation.
Okay. Definitely awake now.
That's impossible.
Tombs project.
Oh, no you don't.
Well, that's new.
Sarah?
Sarah, you there?
I'm here. What's wrong?
I've got something weird on my computer. It tripped a security alarm.
Define weird.
I think somebody's in the system.
Are you sure?
No. That's why I'm calling the smarter scientist.
Good answer.
Can you come take a look?
I'm on my way.
Who are you?
Boundary control.
No, no, no.
Please tell me you didn't break something.
I was asleep.
You called me in here to admit that?
No. That was my defense.
Against what?
Whatever this is. I was reviewing yesterday's test results.
You were sleeping.
I was reviewing them internally.
With your eyes closed?
It's an advanced technique.
Jack.
Right. Problem. I got an unauthorized access warning. I checked the network monitor and saw a connection I didn't recognize, but it disappeared before I could trace it.
And then?
It opened the TOMBS directory.
By itself?
Yep.
You locked the terminal?
And?
It unlocked itself.
I know.
Can I take your chair?
I'm sitting here.
Let me have your chair and get another chair.
Of course. Anything for you.
You said the connection disappeared?
Almost immediately.
External?
I couldn't tell.
That's reassuring.
I thought so.
These are clean.
Mine too. Whoever it was covered both trails.
Too clean.
That's what I was thinking.
No, you were sleeping.
I was thinking eventually.
You know, you're supposed to be resting.
So are you.
I'm not the pregnant one.
No. You're the one I found asleep at a laboratory terminal.
That's different.
How?
I wasn't uncomfortable?
Fair.
Lately the baby seems to think eleven at night is morning.
Already takes after me.
That's what I'm afraid of.
Tombs array remote initialization request.
Did you do that?
No.
Cancel it.
Request denied.
That's not supposed to happen.
Access revoked.
Your credentials?
Revoked.
You're the project administrator.
Who can revoke you?
Me.
I didn't.
Was that the array?
Stay here.
Absolutely not.
Being thirty-two weeks pregnant does not mean made of glass.
Good.
It means you're carrying something considerably more important than this laboratory.
And you're his father.
So we're both going.
Fine. But stay with me.
That I can do.
Warning. array power above standby threshold.
Control, this is Bennett. Shut down power to TOMBS.
Jack, we were about to call you. We're seeing a massive draw from your building.
How massive?
Fourteen megawatts and climbing.
Fourteen?
Fifteen now.
Yesterday's full test didn't use half that.
What's happening over there?
Possible network intrusion. Cut external access to the laboratory and disconnect TOMBS from the island grid.
Doing it now.
Jack? We disconnected you.
It's still running.
That's impossible.
Tonight's developing a theme.
Backup capacitors?
Not enough for this.
Internal reactor?
Offline.
Then where is it getting the power?
I don't know.
I see it.
You didn't authorize an experiment?
No.
Boundary emitters are active.
Kill them.
They're not responding.
Then we'll do it the old-fashioned way.
Okay.
That worked.
I cut the physical connection.
Apparently TOMBS disagrees.
Machines don't get opinions.
This one seems pretty committed.
Boundary acquisition in progress.
What boundary?
That's wrong.
What?
The target dimensions.
It just hid them.
Or somebody hid them.
Do that again.
I didn't do it the first time.
Mapping access denied.
Boundary around what?
That's what I want to know.
Lena, keep the laboratory isolated. Don't sound a settlement alarm yet.
You sure?
No. But I don't know what we'd be telling people to do, and I don't want anyone running toward whatever this is.
Quiet containment until we know the boundary.
Exactly. If anything changes outside this building, call us.
Understood.
Can we interrupt the boundary?
I'm trying.
Could we overload the emitters?
Maybe.
Maybe good, or maybe everyone-inside-the-field-dies bad?
The second one.
Then let's not.
Come on. Give me something.
Boundary acquired.
No.
Scale factor calculating.
Someone isn't just activating TOMBS.
No.
They're running it.
Give me manual control.
Access denied.
Come on. Give me manual control!
I'll try to interrupt the calculation.
Do it.
Nothing.
Again.
I am.
You okay?
I'm fine.
Sarah.
I'm fine. Keep working.
Scale factor locked.
What does that mean?
Jack?
That's not possible.
What does it mean?
Jack!
Sarah! Are you hurt?
I'm okay. I think. Everything's spinning.
The baby?
Give me a second.
He moved.
Okay.
We're okay.
Did it fail?
TOMBS is offline.
Offline because you stopped it?
No. Offline because it finished.
Finished what?
Anything?
Everything says we're fine. Which means something is very wrong.
Jack! Jack, answer me!
I'm here.
Something happened.
I know. Status?
We've got power. Most systems are responding, but communications are down.
Internal?
External. We can't reach anything beyond the settlement.
Satellite?
Nothing.
Radio?
Try the emergency frequencies.
One second.
Jack, come here.
What is it?
What...
Is that... grass?
Jack, what did TOMBS do?
External cameras.
Can you zoom out?
It is zoomed out.
That's a drop of water.
Was that us?
No seismic event.
Then what was it?
The town...
Boundary event complete.
No.
It took all of us.
Everyone inside the boundary.
The homes?
Yes.
The medical center?
Five hundred people.
Jack...
They don't know.
Bennett.
Jack, what happened?
TOMBS activated. We think the developed zone was inside the boundary.
Think?
The system hid the final coordinates before activation. We only confirmed the result afterward.
And the result is?
It changed our scale.
Lena, go to a window. Don't go outside.
Oh.
What do you see?
I'm not sure. There's a wall behind the east fence.
That's the ground.
I was hoping you wouldn't say that.
Stay inside. Keep the night crew inside too. No general alarm yet. I don't want people pouring into the streets before we know what's out there.
Already locking the exterior doors.
Most of the developed zone still has power. Three localized faults, nothing catastrophic.
That's good.
It is.
It doesn't feel good.
Unit Twelve, this is Bennett. Do not cross the end of the road. Turn around and return to the developed zone.
Doctor, I wasn't planning on crossing it.
Dirt. Grass. A lot of both. And I think the dirt is higher than my vehicle.
Any movement?
Negative. Just... big.
Return to town. Quietly. Security personnel only at the perimeter until we know more.
Understood.
We can't keep this quiet until morning.
But waking everyone right now could be worse.
Then we tell the people who need to know first. Medical. Utility. Security. Anyone already awake.
And everyone else?
We give ourselves enough time to learn what we're waking them up to.
Not long.
No.
The external connections.
Could the sensors just be disconnected?
Where's the rest of it?
You found the intake, didn't you?
We're looking at it.
I checked three boundary crossings. Same thing. Power conduit, water intake, and the old fiber trunk. Everything ends cleanly.
How much water is stored inside the settlement?
I'm calculating consumption now. The tanks were designed as buffers, not as our only supply.
Give us the conservative number when you have it.
I will.
Yes. He's moving.
Please tell me that was something in your building.
It wasn't.
Could that be a branch?
Jack?
Nobody goes outside the developed zone.
Don't.
I didn't say anything.
You were about to.
I was thinking internally.
With your eyes open this time?
Advanced technique.
We have a water estimate.
How bad?
At current normal consumption, bad. With emergency restrictions, considerably less bad.
How long?
Several days before we have to start making uncomfortable decisions. Longer if we shut down nonessential industrial use and recycle aggressively.
Already started.
I like her.
So do I.
I can hear you.
Any more shadows?
Nothing clear. Security logged three vibrations since the last one. They don't match anything on the local seismic sensors.
They're not regular.
No. But they're moving.
Moving?
Or whatever is causing them is.
Please tell me we're not using the phrase whatever is causing them in any public announcement.
Nobody's making a public announcement yet.
Good.
Still nothing?
The logs are too clean.
Like the security logs before activation.
Exactly like them.
Could TOMBS erase that itself?
It could delete logs if an administrator ordered it.
But you didn't.
No.
Then whoever did this had more than remote access.
They had control.
Before you start, yes, the station is staffed, yes, the grid is stable, and yes, I locked the door.
I wasn't going to ask.
I was going to ask two of those.
It looks disappointingly normal for a machine that ruined everyone's night.
Give it time.
Doctor Bennett?
That's me.
Mark Jones, perimeter security. I'm headed to the southern boundary for a visual check, inside the developed zone. Wanted you to know before I go.
I'll be at the vehicle.
I need to go outside.
You didn't even think about it.
I didn't need to. It's dangerous.
I know. But the cameras aren't enough. I've watched that boundary since this started and it hasn't told me anything the sensors couldn't already give me as a number.
So now you want to go stand next to it.

Not into the wilderness. Just the edge, on our side. I'll walk the line, take real environmental readings, and see what's actually there instead of what a camera decides to show me. We need firsthand information, not another feed.
Okay. You can go.
Really?
Don't make me reconsider.
I'll stay here and monitor TOMBS, the perimeter cameras, and your sensor feed the whole time. You won't be out there alone.
I'll help her yell at you if you do something stupid.
Noted.
Air composition, temperature, pressure, particulates, radiation. Anything the unit can measure.
And don't cross the line.
I wasn't planning to.
Intentionally.
I'm joking.
Try harder.
Keep safe.
Safe? You're the one leaving and going outside.
I know. I still want you safe.
That's sweet of you. But I need you to be safe. I'll be fine in here.
Both of you.
Both of us.
Love you.
Love you too. Now go, before I change my mind.
Stay on our side.
I'll stay on our side. I promise not to make friends with the grass.
Going.
You still there?
Still here. Still boring.
Good. Keep it boring.
Funny thing about tonight. Usually when your problems get smaller, that's good news.
Not tonight.
Not even a little?
I heard that.
That's grass.
Apparently.
Readings?
Air is normal. Temperature difference is negligible. Pressure is normal.
Radiation?
Background.
My hand is still on our side.
You are genetically incapable of saying that reassuringly.
That is deeply unpleasant.
It's water.
That doesn't make it less unpleasant.
Don't touch it.
I wasn't going to.
For once, I believe him.
Hey Jack, what's that look like to you?
I don't know. What do you think?
I don't know. That's why I asked you.
Fair. It's long. Curved. Kind of like a moon.
UFO?
It's not a UFO, Mark.
Is that plastic?
...Fingernail?
Yeah. Actually — yeah.
Jack, that's a fingernail.
Toenail or thumbnail?
Does it matter?
A little.
We're done. Let's move.
Jack, what's happening?
Something's coming.
Go.
Still attached.
You said thin legs.
I said I saw something that looked like thin legs.
How many?
How big?
That's why we left.
For the record, I support running away from unidentified giant things.
We didn't run.
We ran.
I like him.
Anything useful?
Everything outside the boundary tested normal.
Normal for us?
Normal atmosphere. Same composition, same pressure, same temperature within the sensor's tolerance.
Then physically, we can breathe out there.
Probably.
Probably isn't going in the public announcement either.
I hate that.
Everyone hates that.
Good. I wanted to make sure I was contributing.
Leg?
Go back.
Stop.
What is it?
Could be an insect.
How big are we?
Small enough.
That is not a measurement.
It's the one I have right now.
We can calculate it.
What are you looking for?
The scale target.
You already have it.
I have the result.
Can you tell what they entered?
Most of it was scrubbed.
Most?
Target height normalization.
In normal-person language?
TOMBS wasn't simply told to make the settlement smaller.
It was given a target scale.
Meaning whoever did this chose how small?
That's what I'm trying to confirm.
What does it say?
If the transformation is uniform, an average adult here is somewhere around several millimeters tall.
Several?
Roughly.
I'm fine. Keep going.
Doctor Bennett, this is Doctor Mercer. Did your lab cause that vibration a little while ago?
That is not the answer I wanted.
It's not the one I wanted to give. Any damage?
Nothing serious. One patient woke up frightened, two nurses felt the floor move, and half my overnight staff are arguing about whether we had an earthquake.
Local sensors show no seismic event.
Then why am I looking at grass taller than the medical center?
You looked outside.
Jack, I work nights. Looking outside occasionally is one of the perks.
We had a TOMBS boundary event. The developed settlement's been reduced in scale relative to the surrounding island. We're still working out by how much.
Say that again.
The town got smaller.
That was not better.
What do you need from medical?
For now, keep your overnight staff inside. Check backup power, medical gases, water pressure, and anything that crosses the edge of the developed zone. Don't wake patients unless you need to.
And when they wake on their own?
We're working on that.
Understood. Jack. How long before the rest of the settlement knows?
Not long.
Then don't wait too long to tell me what to do about it.
Dawn's coming.
We can't keep this to Lena, security, and one very unimpressed doctor forever.
We just need a little more before we lose the choice.
For what it's worth, I'd rather know what that is before we wake everyone up to look at it.
Same.
Could the system have picked that number randomly?
Could it have been an accident?
The activation itself could have resulted from corrupted commands. But a specific target scale is different.
The boundary wasn't centered on TOMBS.
It wasn't a radius.
It follows the town.
Why include that?
Wastewater processing.
And that?
Backup substation.
Somebody knew the layout.
More than the layout.
They knew what counted as developed infrastructure.
There's another copy.
Of what?
The activation sequence.
Can you read that?
Eventually.
Search for the boundary coordinates.
Loaded from where?
Three weeks ago.
Could that be wrong?
Not on both systems.
So someone prepared this three weeks ago?
Can you see who created it?
He didn't.
I know. I'm asking why the computer thinks he did.
Where were you?
Three weeks ago?
At that time.
I wasn't in the laboratory.
You were both at the community center.
For almost two hours.
This didn't start tonight.
Phase one?
Okay. That felt closer than the last one.
I don't see anything.
Then what hit the ground?
I'll check the perimeter.
Not alone.
Wasn't planning to be.
Nothing else?
Not yet.
That's not the reassuring answer I was hoping for.
It doesn't mean there isn't a phase two. It only means whoever planted this only labeled the one file they thought nobody would find.
Even more reassuring.
If phase one was the boundary, choosing what to shrink and how much, what's left for a phase two?
Phase one already happened. It didn't need anything running afterward to keep working. The boundary's already set.
So it's not a location. It's something that still has to trigger.
Or something waiting on a timer.
A trigger needs two things. A condition, and a target.
The condition could be anything. Time. A command. Someone doing something specific without realizing it.
That's not comforting.
I didn't say it to comfort you.
Can the target be something that already happened? Or does it have to be something we haven't done yet?
I don't know. That's the part I don't like.
There's a lot of parts you don't like tonight.
Feels like a long list.
Could it target a person?
Why would you ask that?
Because if I were planning something this careful, I wouldn't waste it on a building.
Whatever hit the ground, it's gone. There's a mark out here the size of a dinner plate. Pressed straight down. No drag marks. No trail leading in or out.
Something landed and didn't walk away.
Or something big enough that one footstep doesn't leave much of a trail to follow.
I liked it better when the worst thing out there was a fingernail.
You didn't like that either.
No. But at least I understood it.
Somebody want to catch me up?
Phase one. As in, there's a two.
We don't know that yet.
You don't sound like you believe that.
Jack. Two more patients are awake. One of them heard the tremor and won't stop asking what caused it.
What did you tell her?
That we're looking into it. Which is what I told the last two people who asked, and it stopped working about twenty minutes ago. How much longer am I supposed to say nothing?
Not much longer.
You said that an hour ago.
Jack, I trust you. That's the only reason I haven't paged the whole settlement myself. Don't make me regret it.
She's not wrong.
I know that too.
We tell three more people. Department heads. People who can help without starting a panic.
And if one of them panics anyway?
Then we handle that when it happens. We can't keep running this with four people and one extremely patient doctor.
Five. You're forgetting me.
Four people, one doctor, and a security officer who ran from a shadow.
It had legs.
So do horses. You don't see me running from those.
Horses don't vanish behind a ridge in half a second.
Neither do I, usually. Tonight made an exception.
What are you doing?
If they hid one file for three weeks, I don't think they stopped at one.
You think there's more?
I think somebody patient enough to plant this three weeks in advance doesn't leave loose ends.
That's not a TOMBS component.
Then what is it?
A maintenance tablet. Logged into the network for six minutes, three weeks ago. Same day as the boundary file.
The same day you and Sarah were at the community center.
So somebody used a maintenance tablet to plant a boundary file while wearing your credentials.
That's what it looks like.
Where was the tablet?
The equipment shed by the north pumping station.
That's inside the boundary.
Somebody who works here did this.
Or somebody used a tablet that belongs here. That's not the same thing.
It's close enough to keep me up at night.
This isn't going to give us a name.
Half these people I know. The other half I've waved at in the hallway and never learned their name.
That's not helpful.
I know. I'm hoping it becomes helpful if I keep looking.
Then we need something that will. If someone used that tablet without checking it out properly, there might be a badge location ping from whoever was closest at the time.
You can do that?
I can try.
Every door in this building logs an entry. If someone walked in without using the tablet's own credentials, their badge still would have opened something along the way.
Unless they didn't need a badge.
Everyone needs a badge for this building.
Everyone who's supposed to be here.
For what it's worth, the door logs would still catch a tailgater. Somebody walking in right behind a badge that already opened it.
Would they?
Camera catches the door, not just the badge reader. I can pull that footage too, if it helps.
It might. Add it to the list.
The list is getting long.
The night's getting long too. They're keeping pace.
Pull up every perimeter sensor from the last hour. Not just south.
Looking for what?
Anything that moved and shouldn't have.
You're going to want to see this.
Two impacts. Different locations.
Or the same thing, moving.
Moving how fast?
If those are the same source, it covered that distance in under fifteen minutes.
I'm going back out.
Not alone.
I wasn't planning to be alone. I was planning to take you.
Ten minutes. Cameras stay up the whole time, and you check in every two.
Find that badge ping.
Go.
Dawn's not far.
I noticed.
That mean anything to you? Scientifically?
It means we're running out of dark to hide in.
You scared, Jack?
Good. Means you're paying attention.
Sensor error?
No. Just a lighter touch than the other one.
Lighter how?
I don't know yet.
Jack. I found the badge.
Whose?
I need you back here first.
The badge belongs to a groundskeeper. Retired two years ago.
Retired?
And the badge itself was reported lost eight days before the incident. Facilities has a ticket for it and everything.
So it's not a person. It's a decoy.
Or somebody found it and never turned it back in.
Either way, it doesn't give us a name. It gives us proof that whoever's behind this thought two steps further ahead than we did.
So we're back to nothing.
We're back to nothing with better questions. That's not the same as nothing.
Feels close enough right now.
They didn't just plan the boundary. They planned for us finding the trail.
You're still standing. That's something.
Barely.
Barely counts.
Does it?
Tonight it does.
That's...
Yeah.

This is Aiden, over at the greenhouse. I don't, I need someone to tell me I'm not losing my mind, because there's a spider out here the size of a delivery truck and it is not moving, and I really need somebody to explain that to me right now.
Aiden, stay where you are. Don't approach it. We're on our way.
On your way to do what, exactly?
To explain. Just stay put.
That's not an answer!
I know. It's the best one I've got right now.
That's it. We can't wait for department heads anymore. People are already finding out on their own.
Then we stop trying to control when they find out, and start deciding what we tell them once they do.
I'll get the department heads moving.
Start with medical. Mercer's earned that much.
Already planned on it.
I'll pull every camera we've got. If people are going to see this, they should see it clearly instead of piecing it together out of panic.
How long to put together something people can actually understand?
Depends how much you want to tell them the truth versus how much you want them to stay calm.
Both. In that order.
Then twenty minutes. Maybe less.
Ready?
Medical first. Doctor Mercer, this is Jones. Doctor Bennett wants you briefed in person. I'll have someone at your door in ten minutes.
I've been briefed. I looked out the window.
Then consider this the official version.
Is the official version any better?
No, ma'am.
Wonderful. I'll put the coffee on.
Morning, sir. Inside, please. Doors closed.
What is that?
Grass.
That's not grass.
Believe me, I had the same conversation with myself last night. Inside, please. There'll be an announcement soon.
Lena has the greenhouse cameras. There are two on the outside wall, one inside. I can see Aiden. He's standing very still in the middle aisle.
Good. Is the spider still there?
It hasn't moved since he called.
Can you see it clearly?
Clearly enough that I'd rather not.
For the record, I'm with Aiden. That's bigger than a delivery truck.
You're both exaggerating.
You haven't seen it yet.
You want me to go first?
I want neither of us to go first.
Noted. I'll go first.
Aiden, I'm Jack Bennett. We talked on the radio.
You said you'd explain.
I will. First, put that down.
No.
What's the plan with that, exactly?
If it comes through the glass, I spray it.
That fogger is meant for aphids. If you sprayed that thing with it, it might not even notice. And if you fill this building with insecticide, you're the one who has to breathe it.
Thank you.
I didn't put it down.
That's a start.
Okay. That's not a delivery truck.
Are you serious?
It's more like a car. A small car.
It looked bigger when it was looking at me.
It's still looking at you.
Thank you, Officer, that's very helpful.
Sarah, are you seeing this?
I'm seeing it. Jack, it's tracking you. Every time you move, the front of its body turns a little.
Wonderful.
It's a jumping spider.
You know what it is?
I know what it is when it's the size of a pea. We like them in here. They eat aphids, whiteflies, all the stuff that gets into the seedlings. We never spray when we see one. They're friendly.
Friendly.
When they're the size of a pea.
You said that.
It bears repeating.
If they're hunters, why isn't it hunting?
Because it's cold. They hunt by sight, in daylight. Mornings like this, they sit in the sun and warm up before they do anything. It hasn't moved since I called you because it's waiting.
For what?
For that.
Then it chose this spot for a reason. Jack, look at the glass.
The grow lights. Aiden, do they run all night?
Every night. The seedlings need eighteen hours.
Then every insect on this side of the island has been flying at your glass since dark. And that is breakfast. Lined up in a window.
So it's not here for us.
It's not here for us yet. It came for them. We just happen to be on the other side of the menu.
Okay. So we stay inside, we stay still, and we wait for it to eat and leave.
That's the plan?
That's the plan for the next ten minutes.
What time is it?
Six fifty-eight. Why?
The vents.
What vents?
The roof vents open on a timer. Every morning. Seven o'clock. To let the heat out.
Can you stop them?
The panel's by the front door.
Aiden. The panel. Now. Slowly.
Slowly or now?
Both.
Those are opposites.
Walk like you're carrying a full cup of coffee across a room full of sleeping kids. I'll be right behind you.
Jack, it's watching him.
I know. Aiden, keep going. Same speed. Don't look at it.
How am I supposed to not look at it?
Look at the tomatoes.
Those three aren't answering.
They won't. Those three are on the west feeder. I isolated it last night. It was one of the three faults.
Can you turn it back on?
Not from here, and not without knowing why it faulted in the first place. If I push power into a damaged line, I could start a fire in a building full of dry seedling trays.
Is there a manual override?
There's a crank on each vent. From the catwalk.
I'll go.
No. I'll go.
Jack.
You're the one who knows what to do down here if something comes through. That's carbon dioxide. Cold, loud, and it'll startle almost anything. If you have to use it, aim at the face, not the body.
You've thought about this.
For about four seconds.
That's longer than I usually get.
Doctor Bennett. Slow is invisible. Fast is food.
Good to know.
I'm serious. That's how they see. Anything that moves fast looks like something to eat.
One.
Jack. It's moving.
Tell me.
It's standing up. It's on the pavement now. It's… it's turning toward the roof.
Toward me?
Toward the fly.
Jack, don't move.
It's gone. Jack, it's gone. It went back into the grass.
You're bleeding.
It's small.
Everything's small. That's the whole problem.
It looked at you.
They do that. When they're small. They look at you like they're thinking about it.
What was it thinking?
That you weren't a fly, probably.
I'll take it.
Jack. It jumped. It didn't walk to the fly. It jumped onto the roof from the pavement.
Pressed straight down.
And no trail. Like the mark you found by the southern perimeter.
What mark?
Something hit the ground outside the settlement last night. Twice. It left a print and no tracks.
That wasn't this one. Or not because it was hunting. Jumpers don't hunt in the dark. They need light to see.
So something else out there jumps.
Or something else out there lands. We don't know yet. Write it down. Both.
Sarah. What did we just learn?
It's an animal. It came here for food, and it took food, and it left. It didn't break in because it didn't want to. It never cared about us. That's rule one. It's an animal. It does what animals do.
Rule two?
Nobody attacks anything. Aiden, that includes you.
Three. No lights shining outward along the edge after dark. The lights brought the insects, and the insects brought the spider.
The seedlings need those lights.
Then we put blackout blinds on the western glass at night. The plants get their light. The island doesn't see it.
Four. Anything an insect can fit through gets closed. Vents, cracks, drains. Doors.
Five. Move slowly near glass.
Six. Nobody goes out alone.
Are you writing that down?
I've been writing since rule one.
Jones, this is Unit Four. Are you near the west side?
Go ahead.
Whatever that bang was, half the west side heard it. I've got people coming out of their houses. They're walking toward the community center. Forty, maybe fifty, and more behind them.
Unit Four, what are they saying?
They're asking for Doctor Bennett. By name.
Fifty people. Asking for you by name. That's either very good or very bad.
Which one do you think?
I think I'll drive fast and we'll find out.
Wait. You're leaving me here?
No. You're coming with us.
What about the seedlings?
They'll survive an hour without you. I'm less sure about the reverse.
I'm leaving now. Lena's staying with the cameras.
Sarah—
You were about to tell me to stay in the control room. I'm thirty-two weeks pregnant, Jack, not thirty-two weeks fragile. And they need to see both of us.
Okay. Meet us at the front steps.
I already planned on it.

If you two are finished, I have something useful. The community center has a microphone in the main hall. I can route it to every public speaker in the settlement. Streets, housing blocks, medical, the utility station. Everyone hears the same thing at the same time.
One message.
One message. No rumors, no versions, no 'my neighbor said.' Whatever you say in there, the whole town hears it.
No pressure.
That's him.
Doctor Bennett!
What's going on?
You keep saying that about everything.
Doctor Mercer. We've met. Mostly by phone.
I'm sorry about the phone calls.
Don't be. You answered them. You're bleeding. She's pregnant. You've both been up all night. After this, you're both coming to medical.
You especially.
You were inside a building with a machine that just did this to a town. Humor me.
Lena?
You're live everywhere.
Good morning. My name is Jack Bennett. I run the TOMBS project at the laboratory. Some of you know me. Most of you probably just know the building.

Last night, around eleven o'clock, TOMBS activated without authorization. We tried to stop it, and we couldn't. When it finished, it had changed the size of everything inside the developed settlement. Every building. Every street. Every one of us.
The grass outside didn't grow. We got smaller.
I'm going to tell you what we know, what we don't, and what we need you to do. Then I'll take questions. I promise I'll take questions.
Report it. To who? Pest control?
To security. Mark Jones and his officers.
Hi.
Why don't we attack it?
Lena, play the greenhouse.
Is that you?
What did you do?
I stood very still and tried not to look like a fly.

That's why we don't attack. Because it wasn't attacking us. It came for the insects on the glass, and it took one, and it left. We don't know yet what else is out there. Until we do, we don't start fights we can't finish.
It looked right at him. I was there. It looked at him and it left.
How small are we?
Small enough that a fingernail clipping at the edge of town is longer than I am tall.
Can you put us back?
I don't know. I haven't tried. And I'm not going to try until I understand exactly what it would do. If I get that wrong, I don't get a second chance, and neither do you.
Then call for help. Call the mainland.
We've tried. Every outside channel is silent. Satellite, radio, everything. We're still working on why.
My daughter's in Boston. At school. She's going to call me tonight. What happens when she calls?
I don't know that either. I'm sorry.

Paul Harlan. I run the machine shop. I've kept half the machinery in this town running since before most of you got here. You've been very honest up there, Doctor. I'll give you that. You don't know how small, you don't know how to fix it, you don't know why the radio's dead.
That's right.
So let me ask you something you should know. You said it activated without authorization.
Machines like that don't switch themselves on. Somebody switched it on.
So who was it?
Somebody did.
TOMBS didn't fail last night. Somebody activated it on purpose. They did it with my credentials, and they did it while locking me out of my own system. It wasn't me. I don't know who it was yet.
Your credentials.
So it was your password that did this.
It was my password that somebody else used. That's not the same thing, and I know exactly how that sounds.
It sounds like the lab is telling us the lab didn't do it.
It sounds like that because it's true. I was with him. When it started, we were both in the laboratory trying to stop it. We pulled the shutdown lever. It kept running.
With respect, ma'am, you're his wife.
With respect, Mister Harlan, would I be standing up here next to him if I thought he'd done it?
What else do you know?
More than I'm going to say on this microphone.

Listen to me. Every speaker in this settlement is carrying my voice right now. That's what we wanted. One message, everyone hears the same thing. But it means that if the person who did this is in this town, they're hearing it too.
I'm not going to tell them what we've found. I'm not going to tell them what we're looking for. When I know who it was, you'll know. All of you. That's a promise.
And until then, the lab investigates the lab.
No. Security investigates. Mark Jones and his officers. They report to the whole settlement, not to me.
News to me. Fine.
I want to see what they find. Me, not a summary.
You'll see everything that won't tip them off. Which is most of it.
Most.
Most.
What about food? I've got a two-year-old who eats like a grown man.
The kitchens and the stores are counting everything this morning. I don't have a number for you yet. When I do, it'll come over these speakers, the same as this.
Is there enough?
Today, yes. Beyond that, I won't guess.
I don't believe any of it.
No offense, Doctor. A video of a spider. Grass out the window. I could make that video. I'll believe it when I walk to the end of the road and look.
Nobody walks to the end of the road.
Then how am I supposed to believe you?
Lena, can you give him the western road? Live.
Give me five seconds.
That's live?
That's live. That's the cart Facilities parks there every night. You've walked past it.
What do we do? Right now. Today. Not the rules. What do we actually do?

Today, we count. Water, food, medicine, fuel, everything. We find out exactly what came with us and what didn't. If you have a skill, tell security, and they'll find you something to do with it. If you don't, stay home, check on your neighbors, and keep the lights off at the edge tonight. Nobody's going to fix this by lunchtime. But nobody's going to face it alone, either.
That's all I have. The utility station will post the water limits by noon. Lena, you can turn me off.
Gladly.
Well. Nobody threw a chair.
The day's young.
That was the right answer. About keeping things back.
Paul didn't think so.
Paul thinks it was the right answer too. He just doesn't like it.
I'd rather have him asking questions than not.
If you're calling to review my performance, I'd rather wait.
It was good. That's not why I'm calling.
What's wrong?
Nothing's broken. I want to be clear about that. I've just been watching the water system while you talked.
And?

And the second you said the word restricted, the whole settlement turned on its faucets. Kitchens, showers, laundry, bathtubs. I've never seen a draw curve like it. We've used more water since then than we did in the entire night.
People are filling their bathtubs.
Every bathtub in town, from the look of it. And every pot, every bottle and every bucket they own.
We told five hundred people the water was running out.
And five hundred people did the most reasonable thing in the world.
How fast is it going down?
Fast enough that if I don't do something in the next ten minutes, the limits I post at noon are going to be a lot smaller than the ones I promised you.
Lena. What can you do in ten minutes?
Short of shutting the water off entirely? I can drop the pressure. Block by block. The faucets still run, they just run slowly. Very slowly.
How slowly?
Filling a bathtub would take most of the morning. Filling a glass would take about as long as it does now if you're patient.
What happens to the people who didn't fill anything yet? The ones who were actually listening to the part about restrictions?
They get a slow faucet like everyone else. Nobody gets cut off. Nobody gets ahead any further than they already are.
Keep full pressure at medical.
Already planned on it.
The kitchens, too. And your station.
Done. Housing blocks first, then the workshops. Mark's people are going to get calls.
Lots of calls?
Every single person in town who was halfway through filling something.
Somebody want to tell me why my officers are suddenly getting reports that the water's broken?
It's not broken. It's slow on purpose.
Can I tell them that?
Tell them it's slow so there's enough for everybody. Tell them the limits come at noon.
Unit Four says a man in Block C is very upset about his bath.
Tell Unit Four that a man in Block C is going to have the cleanest emergency in the settlement.
Medical. Now.
Lena needs me at the utility station.
Lena has your wrist. The utility station has walls. Neither of them is going anywhere. Your hand is bleeding through a rag that has now been through a greenhouse roof and a town meeting.
Then it will take very little time to fix.
Glass?
The greenhouse roof.
Of course it was.
Four stitches. Keep it dry. Which, today, should be easy for everyone.
You're next. Don't think I've forgotten.
I would never.
Draw's down to half what it was ten minutes ago. Complaints are up about four times. I'd call that a trade.
Keep it there.
Planning on it.
There you are.
He's annoyed with you.
He's been annoyed with me all night. He kicked me during the activation.
Good. A baby who's annoyed is a baby who's paying attention.
Heartbeat's strong. Size is right where it should be. Movement's good.
What?
Your blood pressure's a little high.
How high?
High enough that I'd like to see it lower, and not so high that I'm going to panic about it. You've been on your feet for nine hours in a crisis. I'd be more worried if it were perfect.
So it's fine.
So it's a little high. I want you resting. I want you drinking your full share of water. And I want to check it again tonight.
Resting where?
Somewhere with a chair.
The utility station has chairs.
The utility station has a crisis.
Every building in this town has a crisis. At least at the utility station, I can be useful while I sit in one of its chairs.
Is she always like this?
Since the day I met her.

Fine. Mark drives you. You sit. You do not climb anything, carry anything, or argue with anyone for more than five minutes at a time. If you feel a headache, dizziness, anything strange with your vision, you call me. Not him. Me.
Deal.
It wasn't an offer.
Draw curve's flattening. You'll want to see this in person. I'm heading to the station now. The gauges there are older than the sensors, and I trust them more.
We're on our way.
Good. There's something else you should know before you get here.
Go ahead.
The machine shop's water was shut off last night with the rest of the industrial lines. Somebody just noticed.
Let me guess.
Five minutes. I'm allowed to argue for five minutes.
Then I'll go first.
You shut off my shop.
Lena shut off every nonessential industrial line last night. Yours was one of them.
Nobody asked me.
Nobody asked anybody. It was the middle of the night and the town had just shrunk.

My lathes run on coolant. Coolant is water. Half my machines are sitting there with jobs clamped in them, and if they sit dry long enough, I'm going to lose parts I can't make again. Not with what's left in this town.
How much water do you need?
Not much. Not every day.
Then tell Lena. She'll put it on the list. But I'm going to be honest with you, it won't be at the top.
Where will it be?
Below drinking, below medical, below cooking. Above washing cars.
I'm not trying to steal anybody's drinking water.

My night shift was on the floor when that machine went off. They didn't get home in time to fill any bathtubs. They're going to get the same slow faucet as everybody else, and some of their neighbors are going to be sitting on a bathtub full of water.
Come inside. You should hear the numbers.
Oh good, everybody. Sit down, Sarah.
I've been told.
Then do it.
Two main tanks. Drinking water. When they're full, they hold about five hundred thousand liters together. Plus the fire reserve, which nobody touches unless something's burning.
That's a lot.
It would be, if they were full. They weren't. They're never full at night.
We use water all day. The tanks drop. Then every night, between midnight and five, they refill from the reservoir.
And TOMBS cut the intake at eleven.
At eleven. Right before the refill. The tanks were close to the lowest they ever get.
How much is in them now?
About three hundred and fifty thousand liters. After this morning.
That still sounds like a lot.
Normal use is about a hundred thousand a day. Showers, laundry, cooking, the greenhouse, the shops. Everything.
Three and a half days.
At normal use. Yes.
So we don't use water normally.
Emergency guidance says a person can get by on about twenty liters a day. Drinking, cooking, a little washing. That's not comfortable. But it's enough.
Five hundred people.

Ten thousand liters a day for homes. Medical needs its own, about three thousand. The kitchens, another two. Call it fifteen thousand a day. Toilets get flushed with a bucket of used washing water, not from the faucet.
That leaves the greenhouse. Aiden irrigates every morning.
From the drinking tanks. It's a big piece of normal use. Bigger than the kitchens.
Then don't use drinking water for it.
The wastewater plant treats everything that goes down the drains, doesn't it? Not to drinking quality. But clean enough for plants.
It does. The treated water goes out to a holding tank and gets released.
Then stop releasing it. Run a line from that tank to the greenhouse irrigation. I can make you the fittings. My night shift can lay the pipe.
That would take the greenhouse off the drinking water entirely.
Give me my night shift and a day.
You'll have them. And your coolant goes on the list.
Fifteen thousand a day. Twenty-three days.
A little over three weeks. If nothing leaks. If nothing breaks. If nobody cheats.
Somebody always cheats.
Then a little less than three weeks.
That leaves Paul's night shift. And everyone else who didn't fill a bathtub.
Can we take the water back?
Knock on five hundred doors and tell people to drain their bathtubs into a truck? We'd lose more trust than water.
Then what?

We don't take it. It's theirs. Whatever's already in a bathtub or a bucket is that household's own. But nobody gets more than twenty liters a day from the faucets, whether they filled a bathtub or not. And we put a drinking-water point at the community center, where anyone who runs short can fill a jug. No questions. Just their name in a book.
So the people who filled their tubs got ahead.
For a few days. After that, everybody's the same.
It's not fair.
No. It's just less unfair than anything else we could do this morning.
My guys can live with that.

Two supply windows a day. An hour in the morning, an hour in the evening. Full pressure during those windows, a trickle the rest of the time. Twenty liters a person. Medical and kitchens on their own allowance. Toilets flushed with washing water. Greenhouse on treated water once Paul's line is in. Drinking point at the community center.
It's eleven fifty-two.
Then you're on.
We're counting the tanks.
That's what we're supposed to be counting.
I know. But we're only counting the water inside.
Last night. At the edge. There was a drop of water out there as tall as I am to the ribs.
One drop. On one blade.
How many blades are out there, Jack?
How far?
Half past six. When the light first hit the grass.
Every morning. That's there every morning.
Lena, can you get Aiden?
He's on his way over with Unit Four. Paul's crew is at the greenhouse measuring for the new line, and Aiden didn't trust them not to drown his seedlings.
Oh. That's dew. Some of it. And guttation.
Gutta-what?

Guttation. At night, plants push extra water up through their roots, and it comes out at the tips of the leaves. Those big ones at the ends, those are the plant's own water. The little ones along the edges are dew from the air.
Is it drinkable?
The dew's basically clean. The guttation drops have minerals and sugars in them. You'd want to test it. Filter it, at least.
And you'd want to be very careful getting it.
Why?

Because insects drown in it. All the time. In the greenhouse, I find gnats stuck in drops on the leaves every morning. The water grabs them, and they can't push their way back out. That one comes up past your chest. If you fell into it, I'm not sure you'd get out either.
Call that one most of a meter across. Even if I'm generous with the shape, it holds more than two hundred liters.
One drop?
One drop. That's ten people's water for a day. And that screen was covered in them.
So we have three weeks of water in the tanks, and more water than we could ever use sitting just past the end of the road every morning.

Sitting past the end of the road, inside a forest full of things the size of cars. This morning I told that kid nobody even walks to the end of the road. You told the whole town nobody goes past it. Now you're going to stand there and tell me we're going out?
Not today.
When?
Not tomorrow, either. This morning we ran in because we didn't have a choice. This time we plan it.
Plan what, exactly?
A small team. Roped together. On radio, every two minutes, the way you and I did last night. The very edge of the western road and no farther.
And bring back what?
One jug. And a sample for Aiden to test. That's all. If it works once, we know how to do it again.
So when?
First light. When the water's there and the spider's still cold. Back before the sun's off the grass. Nine o'clock at the latest.
And if the spider's not cold?
Then we stand very still and try not to look like flies.
You said that this morning.
It worked this morning.
The day after tomorrow. I want a whole day to plan it. I want to know every single thing that can go wrong before I let anyone stand next to one of those.
Agreed.
I could tell you which plants those are. The ones with the biggest drops. If I could see them up close.
You want to come.
I want to not be useless.
You weren't useless this morning. You knew what it was. Nobody else did.
Measured the greenhouse end. I'll have treated water on those plants by tonight. Tell the kid his tomatoes will live.
Thank you, Paul.
Don't thank me. Put my coolant on the list.
It's on the list.
Higher.
Better.
I said better, not good. Still a little high. I'll be back tomorrow night. Until then, rest. Real rest. Not chair rest.
I rested all afternoon.
You ran a water department from a chair.
You're going out there.
To the end of the road. Not one step farther.
You said that about the boundary last night.
And I came back.
With a fingernail story and a cut hand.
Four stitches. Mercer was very proud of them.
He wants you to come back by nine.
Tell him I promise.
You tell him. He heard your voice on every speaker in town this morning. He'll recognize it.
You up?
I never went down.
Figured. That thing last night. You heard it?
I heard it.
So did the perimeter sensors. Eleven forty, out past where any camera can see. One hit, nothing after. My night officers looked at every feed we've got. There's nothing to look at.
So we don't know.
We don't know. I'm putting it with the others. Planning meeting at nine. Utility station. Bring coffee. Don't bring Sarah.
Morning, Doctor Bennett.
Morning, Mark. I'll be watching on the cameras. Lying down. Doctor Mercer's orders.
Then I'll make sure to look busy.
You didn't sleep.
I watched the grass.
Did it do anything interesting?
It got wet.
Good morning, Paul. Is that for us?
It's for whoever's stupid enough to use it. Your greenhouse line's in. Finished around three.
In the dark. At the edge.
Under tarps. Every lamp pointed at the ground. Your Unit Four stood there all night making sure. He checked twice.
The tomatoes are drinking it. I checked at six. Nothing's wilting.
Told you they'd live.
Before we start. The kitchens sent their count. I'm reading it out at noon, so you might as well hear it first.
Not as bad as water. About six weeks of food, at careful portions. A little longer once the greenhouse starts giving us more than salad.
Then water's still the clock.
Water's still the clock.
Good. Then let's talk about the end of the road.
It's out there. We've seen it. We know it hunts things that move fast. That's one.
Aiden says insects drown in those. Anything that can trap a fly can trap a person. That's two.
The soil past the asphalt is wet in the morning. Wet soil is slippery. Nobody's standing on it. That's three.
We haven't seen one up close. I'd like to keep it that way. Four.
If the radio fails, we come back. We don't wait to find out why. Five.
What's that one?
Somebody decides the plan is a suggestion. Somebody sees a bigger drop two meters farther in and thinks, just this once. That's the one that kills people. That's six.
Nobody's going to do that.
Good. Then it's an easy rule to keep.
Tell me how we get the water.
Not with a cup.

In the greenhouse, when a drop sits on a seedling too long, it rots the leaf. So I wick it off. I touch the drop with a corner of cotton cloth, and the water runs into the cloth on its own. You don't scoop it. You let it soak in.
Why not a cup? A cup's simpler.
Because at our size, water climbs. It'll run up the rim of a cup and over the side and onto whoever's holding it. Same with skin. If that drop touches your hand, it won't fall off. It'll keep coming.

Four meters. Painter's pole from Facilities. The sponge is new, from my parts washer, never been used, so you won't be drinking machine oil. You soak it, you swing it back, you squeeze it into a funnel.
Into what?
A twenty-liter jug. One person's water for a day.
Now it's heavy.
That's a lot of water on the end of a long stick. Don't let it swing.
And you're doing that with one and a half hands.
Mercer said keep it dry.
Mercer's going to love this.
I'll wear a glove.
Wear two.
Three people go. Small, roped, slow. I'm on the rope. I've done this before, and I'm the one who says when we leave. Jack's on the pole.
The man the whole town is waiting on to name a saboteur. You want him standing next to a spider?
I told five hundred people to stay off the edge. If anybody goes, I go.
Then don't fall in.
You're third. You take the sample, and you tell us what we're looking at. We tie the line off to the maintenance cart at the end of the road, and Unit Four stays at the cart and holds it.
And our feet?
Toes on the asphalt. All three of us. Nobody steps onto the soil. Not for a bigger drop, not for a better sample, not for anything.
Sarah's on the line. She says it's important.
Put her on.
I've been going through the greenhouse cameras from this morning. The two on the outside wall. They look along the edge toward the end of the road.
Lena, can you pull up the first outside camera, six forty-five?
I thought that was a seed head. It isn't. Watch.
It's a retreat. They sleep in those. They spin one and come back to it.
It sat there for a quarter of an hour. Then, just before seven, it started hunting. Right along the end of the road.
That's one morning. A cold morning, or a cloudy one, and it could change.
I know. But the water's there from half past six. And the spider comes out when the sun hits the grass.
Half an hour.
It lives there. Right above the end of the road. Every time we go out there, it'll be watching us.
The railing is the cart. The gravel is the road. That drain over there is the edge. Nobody goes past the drain.
It's a very small drain.
Then it'll be very easy to stay away from.
Stop.
Good. That's the word. When I say it, you're a fence post. You don't look around. You don't ask why. You stop.
For how long?
Until I say go.
What if you don't say go?
Then you're a fence post for a very long time.
You hold this. You don't let go of it. If I yell pull, you pull.
Yes, sir.
If you see something coming that we don't, you say so. You don't wait to be sure.
And you don't call me sir.
Yes, sir. Sorry.
You rested.
I lay on that couch all day. I watched cameras. I watched Jack drill water into a bucket on Lena's feed. I've never been so bored in my life.
Good. Keep it that way.
Same as last night.
Same as better, or same as high?
Same as high. Not worse. I'd have liked better. I'll take same.
No protein. That's good. That's the one I was watching for.
So I can stop being bored?
No.
I hear you're going to be holding a wet pole in the morning.
News travels.
Everything travels. It's a very small town. If that gets wet, you come straight to me. Not after you've made your report. Straight to me.
Yes, Doctor.
And if the spider's out early?
We stop. We wait. If it doesn't go back, we come home.
And if the radio goes quiet?
We come home.
And if you see a bigger drop two meters farther in?
You've been talking to Lena.
Lena told me everything. Answer the question.
I leave it there.
Then sleep. You can't hold a pole straight if you've been awake for two days.
Is that normal?
Nothing is normal. That's just loud.
Station, this is Bennett. We're at the cart.
Station hears you. Two minutes, starting now.
I'm lying down. Ask anyone.
Morning.
Morning. Be boring.
That's a robin, I think.
Is it close?
I don't know. I can't tell anymore.
Two minutes. You all still there?
That one's the plant's. At the tip.
Ten minutes of gray. Then the sun.
It's working.
Swing it back. Slow.
Two minutes.
Maybe three liters.
Wipe it. Don't let it reach the glove.
Dew. Not the plant's water. That's the one I want to test.
Good. Now stay off that edge.
There's something in that one.
A midge. It's been stuck there all night.
Dead?
Cold.
Two minutes. Don't answer that.
Pull.
Aiden. Stop moving.
We're done. Back to the cart.
I've got it.
Is everyone all right?
Everyone's all right. Aiden's wet.
And you?
I'm about to be in trouble with Doctor Mercer.
I already called her. She's meeting you at the station. And she says the station counts as straight to her, this once.
Low minerals. Low salt. It's dew, all right. Clean enough to filter and boil. Whether there's anything living in it, I can't tell you today. That takes longer.
Twelve liters. Half an hour. And we nearly lost you.
You didn't.
We're not doing that every morning. I'm telling you now.
We need fifteen thousand a day.
Which is why we can't do it with a stick.
It came down to us.
The drop?

We spent half an hour reaching up for it with a stick. Then the blade bent, and it fell on its own, right onto the asphalt. We don't need to reach the water. We need to make it come down. Shake the blade, and let it fall onto something that catches it.
A trough. Along the end of the road, under the leaf tips.
Paul. You awake?
I am now.
Could you make us a trough? Long, shallow, sitting on the asphalt at the end of the western road.
A gutter. Yes. Give me a day. And I'm putting a collar on that pole of yours. I watched the feed. Water running down to your hands like that, it's a wonder it didn't grab a fistful of you.
Don't thank me. Bump my coolant.
It's seven fifty. You said nine.
I'm early. Don't get used to it.
He kicked. When you said you were coming back.
Tell him I heard. No. I'll tell him myself. Tonight.
It watched us. The whole time. Every pass with the pole, every time you swung it back. It knew exactly where we were. So why didn't it come for us?
Because we were slow.
Not slow. Boring. The midge wasn't.
Which is the problem with your trough. Shaking grass isn't boring. Shaking grass is fast. And fast is food.
Then we do it in the gray. Before the sun. Before it's warm.
Hand.
They held.
Is that good?
It's not bad. Sit still.
If it goes red and hot, or it starts to throb at night, I want to see it the same hour. Not the next morning. I have antibiotics. I would very much like to never open them. I can't make more.
You said that last time.
You're warm. Did you hit your head when you went down?
No. I hit the water. The water hit me.
Then you're going home. Dry clothes, something hot, and four hours of sleep.
I have to start the long test.
Start it. Then sleep.
Eight o'clock tonight. Both of you. Jack, that means your wife and your hand.
Flat. It tastes like nothing.
That's what water tastes like.
I know. I just thought it would taste like something, after all that.
Jack's trough. Five things I don't like about it.
Shaking a blade is fast. Fast is food. Aiden's rule, not mine.
