Yes.
It's off the camera. I can't see it anymore. Go when you're ready. Go slowly.
Relay's up. Station hears you.
I see it, Jack. I see what you see.
Now don't fall in.
It holds.
It goes first. We go down when it comes back up. Not before.
It's at the bottom.
How long does it need?
Five minutes. Then bring it up.
Oxygen's normal. Carbon dioxide's a little higher than up here. That's what you'd expect underground. Nothing flammable. Nothing poisonous.
It's air. It's damp, but it's air.
Say the oxygen again.
Then go. And if that box makes any noise at all, you come back up.
Jack. You said you'd look and come back. Go and look.
There's a wire taped to that cable. A plug on the cage. If the radio goes, you plug in. You'll hear us.
Got it.
Then go down.
I see you. I've got all three of you. You're about a quarter of the way. You're doing fine.
Jack, you're—
—say again—
That's the concrete.
Jack? Jack, say something.
We're down. We're all down.
Okay. Okay. Lights. Show me.
The drawing said a tunnel.
It is a tunnel. For people the size it was built for.
That's the breath. That's what was breathing.
Don't touch it. Not yet. Not a hand, not a boot. I don't know what's in it.
Lena. Are you seeing this?
I'm seeing it. I can't give you a flow rate from a picture.
But it's more than we use.
Nobody stands near the edge. If I slip, you pull my boots. You don't come in after me.
While he's doing that. Jack, turn around. Slowly. All the way.
Aiden's scanner is drawing the gallery. It goes on. Both ways, past where the drawing stops caring. And there's something on the far wall I want you to see.
That's not on the drawing. The drawing has that wall as solid all the way along. I've marked it.
Nobody goes near it.
Nobody was going to.
Mark. Don't move. On your camera. The wall behind the cage. Something's on it.
Centipede. They hunt in the dark. They're fast.
Into the cage. Walk. Don't run.
Four. Up. Now.
Two jars?
Two jars. The third one's down there. It can stay there.
It's hard water. Full of minerals, from running over all that concrete. That's not a problem. It tastes of chalk, that's all.

It has bacteria in it. Not a lot. Ordinary ones. What you'd find in any water that's run over the ground and into a drain. Nothing my kits can find that a filter and chlorine and boiling won't deal with.
Your kits.
My kits. They're not a laboratory.
No, they aren't.

So here's what it is. It's not drinking water. Not yet. First it washes. It flushes toilets. It waters the greenhouse. Every liter of that is a liter that doesn't come out of the tanks. Then it gets treated, and you test it after it's treated, three times, three days in a row, clean every time. Then I'll talk about drinking.

The station has chlorine. For cleaning the tanks. And there's the old irrigation tank behind the building. Nobody's used it since they put the new line in. It's separate from the drinking tanks. Nothing mixes.
Aiden. When it doesn't rain. Does the channel stop?
It hasn't rained since the eleventh. It was running full on the fifteenth. Drains like that pick up water out of the ground, not just off the top. It'll drop in a dry spell. I don't think it stops.
Then we measure it. Every day. Before anyone counts on it.
And how does it get from down there to up here?

No single pump in this town will lift water up that shaft. Sarah's scanner says it's over six hundred meters. A good pump does a hundred. So we do it like a mine. A pump at the bottom pushes up to a drum on a platform. The next pump takes from the drum and pushes up to the next. Electric, every one, because an engine down there fills that tunnel with exhaust and then Aiden's meter says no. A generator in a shed at the grate. Seven pumps, if I can find seven.

Then the hoses. Every hose in town. Fire station, greenhouse, my shop. Up the shaft, along Four's stakes to the road end, down the southern road to the station. It's a long way. But we've got a lot of hose.
How much water?
Thirty liters a minute. Maybe. If the hose holds.

Thirty a minute. Only while people are out there with it. They walk the line first, they're at the grate by nine, they have to start back by half past two to be off the soil by five. Call it ten thousand liters on a good day.
It's not seventeen. It doesn't replace the tanks.
But ten thousand a day we don't take out of them is the difference between running out at the end of this month and running out weeks later. Weeks we don't have now.
Same rules. Daylight. Off the soil by five. If Sarah says stop, we stop.
It's not a house. It's a place to stand.
It's an outpost.
Call it what you want. Don't sleep in it.
Mark. What happens to that hose tonight?
Nothing. It sits there.
In the dark. With slugs. And whatever crossed the road on the eleventh. And seventy-two joints that nobody's looked at since lunch.
Who checks it in the morning? Before anybody walks out along it?
First light. The whole line. Every joint. Before anybody else goes out.
Every joint.
Write it down, Sarah.
I already did.
So we do it like a mine.
One pump at the bottom pushes up to a drum. The next one takes from that drum and pushes up to the next. Every stage only lifts its own bit. Every hose only holds its own bit.
Stage two. Clamped. Nothing on the walls.
Nothing on the walls. I've got the platforms on Aiden's camera.
Bottom first. Then each one wakes up when its drum fills. If one doesn't, the one under it fills its drum and stops. Nothing breaks. It just waits.
Stage two's full. Three's filling. Three's full. Four.
Four's full and five isn't running. The water's at the top of four's drum. It's not going anywhere.
Float's stuck.
Jack. You know the float?
I watched Aiden hang it.
Then go and unstick it. I'll run the winch.
Five's running.
Six. Seven. Jack, come up. You did it. Come up.
It's here. It's coming in. It's cloudy, it's coming in cloudy, it's clearing. It's clear.
It's water. It's coming into my tank.
First chlorine's in. Aiden, I need a jar.
We'll know in the morning.
That's a wet line.
And there's something coming along it. On the road camera. The beetle. From the far side, along the hose. Toward you.
How far?
Four stakes. It's walking.
Three stakes.
Two.
Done.
One stake. Get back. Back along the stakes, now.
Every joint. Every morning.
Every morning.
Clean.
Clean how?
After the filter and the chlorine, nothing my kits can find. Nothing growing. It tastes like a swimming pool and a piece of chalk.
That's one.
Out of three.
Out of three.
So it doesn't go anywhere anyone drinks it. It goes where it doesn't matter if it tastes of chalk.

The old irrigation tank can open into the pipes that feed the community laundry, and the public washrooms' showers and basins, and the kitchens' washing-up. Inside, through the pipes. Nothing poured outside. All of that came out of the drinking tanks until this morning.
So the tanks stop paying for laundry.
And the showers. And the washing-up.
Nine thousand six hundred liters.

A hundred and nineteen thousand. At seventeen a day, that's seven days. But the drinking tanks aren't paying for the laundry anymore, or the showers, or the washing-up. If the line runs every day like today, the town takes about seven thousand a day out of them, not seventeen.
Seventeen days. To the beginning of April.
Nobody crosses the channel. Nobody goes up the gallery or down it past the scanner. And nobody goes near that.
I don't care what it is. Not this month.
People saw the hoses go down the southern road. They saw my crew carry them.
People think the end of the road is where you die. My crew's been past it three days running. It's where you work. Tell them that, when you tell them about the water.
Thirty-four weeks today.
I know.
Anything new?
Sometimes it goes tight. All of it. My whole belly. Maybe half a minute. Then it lets go. It doesn't hurt. Not really. Twice today. Three times yesterday.
That's practice. Your body rehearsing. Normal, at this stage. They come and go, they don't get closer together, they don't get stronger.

Here's what isn't practice. If they come regularly, closer and closer. If they hurt and keep hurting. Any bleeding. Any water. Or he goes quiet when he usually kicks. Any of those, you call me. Not Jack. Not the station. Me. Day or night.
I know the list.
Then say it to me.
And I want something from you.
Anything.
Your wife is going to have this baby here. In this town. With what this town has.

Every delivery on this island was planned with a hospital behind it. Somewhere to send her if anything went wrong. There isn't one now. I've made a list of what I've got. Tomorrow I want to go through it with both of you. Line by line.
What's missing?
More than I'd like.
I can deliver a baby. I've delivered a good many. I want you both to hear that first, because the rest of this is going to sound worse than it is.
Here's what I haven't got. I haven't got a second pair of trained hands. A delivery should have two people who know what they're doing, and this town has one, and it's me.
Go on.

I have some of the drug we give after a birth to stop the bleeding. Not as much as I'd like, and some of it's close to its date. I have a handheld monitor for the baby's heart, the kind you hold against your belly for a minute. I don't have the kind that watches it all the way through labor.
And if he comes out and doesn't breathe on his own straight away, I have a bag and a mask and my own two hands. That's all.
Four things.
I'm not finished.
Then five things. I'm writing them down.
Most babies don't need any of it. Most of them come out loud and pink and furious and need nothing from anyone except a blanket.
I'm telling you because I'd rather have every one of them and not use it.

A second pair of hands. Somebody in this town has done this before. Not as a doctor. A nurse. Somebody who's had five children. Somebody who was a paramedic before they came here. We find out who. The bleeding drug. You said some of it's close to its date. Does the pharmacy here have anything else that does the same job?
Some. Not much.
Then we count it, and you tell us exactly how much you'd want.
The heart monitor. Jack builds things. Paul builds things. The handheld one works. Can it be made to keep working? Strapped on, wired to a screen?
Possibly.
And the breathing.
That one I don't know yet.
No. Neither do I.
Then that's the one we start on first.
You're doing it again.
Somebody has to.
Eight o'clock. Every morning. Here. Twenty minutes. Everyone who runs something. I keep the list.
Water first?
Water first.
Second test was clean. Third one's this afternoon. The line ran nine thousand eight hundred yesterday.

Drinking tanks are down to a hundred and eight thousand. If the third test is clean and Doctor Mercer says yes, the gallery water stops being washing water and starts being water. It doesn't change the sum. We still use more than we pump. But it means every liter of it can go anywhere it's needed.
And if I put a second pump in the same channel, and a second line beside the first one, they stop going down at all.
Another seventy hoses?
Another forty. I'll run it to the hydrant main on the southern road and let the pipes do the rest. Two weeks.
One week.
Ten days.
Ten days.
Food.
Six weeks at careful portions, from the seventh. That's the middle of April.

The greenhouse has been on treated water from the plant since the first week, rationed. It's been growing salad and keeping the tomatoes alive. Now there's gallery water too. I can water everything. And if somebody gives me the back hall of this building and a hundred grow lights, I can put beds in it. Beans. Potatoes. Things that fill you up.
The power's there. The microgrid can take it if the streetlights at the edges stay off.
They're staying off.
Then you can have your hundred lights.
Houses.

The last block on every road. Twenty-two families. They live where the night hunter walks and where the slugs come out. I want them farther in. There are empty houses. People who were off the island when it happened.
Their owners aren't coming back. Not soon. We ask. We don't tell. Anybody who wants to stay, stays, with the rules.
Pell won't move.
Then Pell stays. Unit Four can check on him.
Drinking water. Boiled, for the first week, until I'm sure. Then out of the tap.
The breathing line. You said start there.
I did.
Where do you start?
With people. Five hundred of them. Somebody in this town has kept a baby breathing who wasn't supposed to. A nurse who left nursing. A grandmother. A paramedic who came here to fix pumps.
We don't know, because nobody's ever asked. So tomorrow Lena asks. Over every speaker in town.
And if nobody comes?
Then we build it ourselves.
But somebody will come.

This is the utility station. Doctor Mercer is asking for help. If you have ever delivered a baby, or helped deliver one, or cared for newborns, as a nurse, as a medic, as a parent, as anything, please come to the medical center today or tomorrow. That's all. Thank you.
As anything. That's good. I didn't tell her to say that.
She's been listening to you.
Three. That's three more than yesterday.
It's going to rain. Properly. Not like the drizzle on the eleventh.
I don't know what that looks like, here. Nobody does.
Everyone in by ten. Pumps off, outpost shut. Nobody past any road end. Nobody outside at all. A drop that size hits you, it doesn't make you wet. It knocks you down.
Mark bolted the bottom pump to the floor when they set it, and every platform's clamped to its rung. If the water comes down the shaft, it comes down. They won't go anywhere.
Lena. How much rain falls on a roof?
Depends on the rain.
How much falls on all of them?
A lot.
Then we don't let it run into the drains.
Every container in town with a lid. Bins, barrels, the big kitchen pots, the coolers. Under the downpipes. Filled from the gutters and closed the moment they're full. Lids on.
Covered.
Covered. So nothing breeds in it and nothing comes to drink. A mosquito lays eggs in open water. Out here, the thing that hatches would be as long as I am.
Who tells five hundred people to go out and stand under their gutters?
Nobody goes out. The downpipes come down against the walls. People put the bins at the back doors, fill them through the door, drag them in, and shut the door.
Lena tells them. She's very calm.
Jack. Jack, the downpipes.
Station's taking water through the vents. Small. I've got it. Everybody stay in.
Paul says the wire down the shaft is still live on his meter.
There's a waterfall down my shaft, right onto my platforms. That's what the grate's for. That's what it's always been for. Don't anybody go and look.
Rooftops. The bins, the barrels, everything people caught. About fourteen thousand liters. Every lid we had. The roofs threw away a hundred times that.
It needs boiling. It's not tested. But it's fourteen thousand liters, in one afternoon, in buckets.
The channel's the highest I've measured. It's running fast. It'll drop again, but the ground's full. It'll stay up for days.
It's the twenty-sixth.
At seventeen thousand a day, today's the day it would have read zero.
It says seventy-two thousand. Not zero. Seventy-two. And the rain bins will carry the kitchens for two days.
Paul's second line is half laid. When it's in, I think the tanks go up. Not down. Up.
Lena.
I know. I'm not celebrating. I'm writing it down.
You're Doctor Bennett.
Jack.
Jack. Your security man drinks my tea. He tells me things. He told me about the baby.
My wife made this. Years ago. For a grandchild we never got.
She'd want it used. Not kept. Used.
Thank you, Mr. Pell.
Thirty-five weeks, your man says.
Today.
Good. That's good.
My beans liked the rain. Through the window. I've never seen them so pleased.
Thank you for coming. I'm going to ask you each one question, and I want the true answer, not the helpful one.
Why didn't you ever tell me?
You never asked. And I came here to stop doing it.
Will you do it again?
Once.
For her. Yes.
You'll be runners. When it starts, you fetch, you carry, you boil, you hold the light, and you do what she says before you do what I say. Can you do that?
The injection.
This is what I give after a birth, so the womb clamps down and stops bleeding. I've got this much. Two of them go out of date next month.
And these.
I didn't know we had that many.
Tablets. They do the same job, slower. They don't need a refrigerator, and they keep for years. On the wards where I trained, when the injections ran out, this is what we used.
With these, and the injection, I've got enough. Enough that I'm not afraid of it.
That one is Sarah's. Nobody touches it for anybody else unless it's a life.
That's two.
So it needs to stay where you put it.
And it needs somebody to listen to it the whole time, or something to do the listening.
Strap's easy.
Something to do the listening's your end.
He's all right. Jack. Look at him. He's all right.
He's all right.
Nineteen thousand three hundred.
Pumped. Today. That's more than we use.
It went up.
How much?
Not much. Two thousand. But it went up.
It's never gone up. Not once. Not since the fifth.
That one's the one I care about. The other three are about making sure nothing goes wrong. This one's about what to do if something does.

If he comes out and doesn't breathe well on his own, I have a bag and a mask. That's good for a few minutes. It's not good for an hour. And I have nothing that helps a baby breathe for himself, for longer.
There's a way.

I saw it used where there were no machines. Not here. A long time ago, somewhere that couldn't afford the machines. You need oxygen, which you have, from the concentrator. You need tubing, and a bottle of water, and something to hold the tube under the water at the right depth. The water pushes back. It keeps the baby's lungs open, so he doesn't have to work so hard.
It's simple. It isn't a toy. But it works, if somebody builds it right.
Show me.
Tubing and a bottle. I can build that.
The water pushes back.
The baby breathes out against it. It keeps the little air sacs in his lungs from collapsing between breaths, so he doesn't have to open them again every time.
And the deeper the tube, the harder it pushes.
Yes. So the tube has to be held at exactly the right depth. Not about right. Exactly. Mark the bottle.
That's right. That's what it looked like.

Don't. All that tells us is the bottle does what a bottle does. A doll doesn't breathe. It doesn't get tired, or cold, or go the wrong color. This has never been on a baby, and the first baby it goes on, I'll be watching him, not the bubbles. If it isn't helping, it comes off.
So what's it for?

For after. Only if. Drying him, warming him, clearing his mouth and holding his head right, and Doctor Mercer's bag and mask if he needs breathing for. Those come first, and they're most of it. This is the thing we have for when those aren't enough, and it might not be enough either.
Better than nothing.
Better than nothing. Not a hospital.
Head down.
Where he should be. A good size. Not too big.
Hundred and forty on the screen. Your pulse is about eighty. So it's counting him, not you. Good.

It's a good machine. It isn't a trained ear. It can lose him when she moves, and it can find her heart instead of his and count that just as happily. It tells us when to look. It doesn't tell us he's well. Somebody who knows what a baby sounds like listens to it too.
So he's doing everything right.
He's doing everything right. You're doing everything right.
And for once, so is the town.
It's started. Five minutes apart.
Copy.
Bring her.
Four minutes.
Four minutes if nobody's in the street. Three and a half if I don't stop for anybody.
Lena. Now.
Eleven seconds.
Lena. Thank you. Put it back.
You could have told me you were going to do that to your own building.
Then it wouldn't have been a test.
I was afraid of that night. Not the baby. The night. The dark and the town and nothing to fall back on.
I'm not afraid of the night anymore. I'm only afraid of the things nobody can plan for. Which is what every doctor is afraid of, everywhere. That's not a reason to stop. That's just the job.
I don't know what to do with my hands.
You could rest.
Aiden. It's Sarah. That gnat in your jar. You said you wanted to know what it was eating.
Did you find out?
That's its gut.
I touched a test strip to it. Sugar. The water the plants push out of their leaf tips at night, the same sticky water you see dried there at first light, when the flies come. That's what it lives on.
So the plants feed the gnats.
And the gnats get stuck in the drops, and they kick, and the spider takes the ones that kick.
And then the spider drinks the drops. It's all one thing. It's one machine, and we're standing in the middle of it trying to steal the water.
How much of that do you know, and how much do you think?
That's the problem.
A month of it. Everything I've seen. Everything anyone's told me.

But I saw it when I happened to be looking, and I wrote it down when I happened to have paper. I don't know what's normal. I don't know what's rare. I don't know if the slugs came because it was damp, or because I only ever look when it's damp.
Then we look at the same things, at the same times, the same way, every day. And we write it down the same way.
Nine road ends. Nine cameras. Four times a day.

First gray, because that's when the drops are there and everything comes out. Mid-morning. Late afternoon. And dark, as long as there's a light to see anything by. Every time, somebody watches each camera for ten minutes and writes down everything that moves. What it is, if they know. How big, against something we know. What it's doing. Where it goes.
On one sheet.
On one sheet. The same sheet, every time, every road.
And nobody goes out to look. Nobody gets closer. It's watching. Only watching.
Who watches? That's thirty-six watches a day.
People who can't carry hoses.

People with bad backs. People who are eighty-one and don't want to move house. The woman from the kitchens, with her grandchildren at home and bored out of their minds. They watch from their couches. I watch from mine. I keep the book.
What do we call it?
It's your box.
The Field Book. That's what it is. A field book. Except we can't go into the field.
Then it's a field book from a couch.
It's the Field Book.
I'll take one. Somebody should who's seen the things.
Jack. Come here. Now. Slowly.
It's the robin.
It's hunting.
Where's Four?
Unit Four. Where are you?
At the outpost. Inside. With the door shut. I heard it land.
Stay there.
I'm staying.
Every morning. Four, and whoever's with him. Walking that line in the open. In daylight.
In daylight. Because the night's when the hunters come out.
The night's when the hunters we knew about come out.
Aiden was right. It's one machine. And we didn't know where the top of it was.
Line walk goes under the stems where it can. Where it can't, it goes fast and it goes together.
And I want a roof over the open stretch. Anything. Tarps on poles. Something a bird looks at and sees a roof.
A roof I can do.
It's a timetable.

It's a timetable. The flies come at first gray, every wet road, on every tip that hangs over asphalt. The day spider comes out when the light does. The robin comes at mid-morning, and only at the southern road, because the soil's open there and it can see. The slugs come on damp nights; you can see their trails at gray. The night hunter goes home at first gray, every time.
And the northern roads are dry.
Aiden thinks the ground falls away from the road there. The water runs off before anything comes to drink it.
It's a guess. But it's a guess we can check now, because it's the same every day.
It sees a roof.
It sees dead grass. Which it's not interested in. I asked Aiden.
It hides us. It doesn't stop it. Nobody forgets that.

Food. The kitchens counted again on Monday. With what the greenhouse is giving now there's water for it, careful portions go to the end of the month, maybe a few days past. Aiden's beans in the back hall are up. Nothing to eat off them for three weeks.
Then food is the next list.
Food is the next list.
Thirty-seven weeks. That's early term. If he came now, I wouldn't be worried.
He's not coming now. He's comfortable.
Head down. Pressure holding.
Good. I'd still like him to stay where he is a little longer. Another two weeks would suit me fine. But if he doesn't, we're ready. That's a sentence I didn't think I'd say in this town.
How long's that been there?
Mr. Pell says there were two at first gray. He drew them. Then there were ten.
Now there's that.

They follow a scent. The first one to find food lays a trail on the way home, and the others walk on the trail, and every one that finds food lays more. It's not that the bins are interesting. It's that one ant found them, and told everyone.
Then we take the bins away.
And the trail. If the trail's still there, they'll keep coming.
They live in there.
Mark said nobody goes near it.
I'm not going near it. I'm going to the records building.
Everything else down there matches. Every tile. Every rung.
Except that.
The modules are whole sections of the island. That's a room.
Or a very small one. A module somebody stopped drawing.
It was there.
It was on the drawing. And then it wasn't.
So it's a door.
It was a door. On one drawing. Three revisions. The oldest has it. The two newer ones don't. Nothing in the archive says why.
I don't know that number.
That's where the centipedes go. Every sheet. They come out of that wall and they go back into it.
So what. Let them have it.
That's the question.

Here's what I know. Behind that wall, there's a room nobody's been in. It's a few minutes' walk from the pumps that keep this town in water. Every pump crew that goes down there works with their back to it. And something that hunts in the dark lives in it.
I don't want to know what's in it because I'm curious. I am curious. But that's not why.
I said not this month.
It's April.

Here's how. Daylight hours only. Three people. Lights. The gas meter goes first, at the door, before anybody does. Sarah on every camera. And the moment anything's wrong, anything at all, everybody comes back. Nobody argues. Nobody finishes what they were doing. They come back.
And how do you get across the channel? It's wider than the station yard. I'm not building a bridge over that.
You don't have to.
It's on the oldest one. And the newest one. And it's on Aiden's scanner. We just never went that way.
It's a grating. Like the one over the shaft. Laid over the channel so the people who built it could walk across.
The gaps are wide, for us. But the bars are wide too. You could walk across on one.
On one bar. Over that.
With a rope. Tied off at both ends. Like the road.
What about the things that live there?

Every time the bottom pump's light has come on, the ones on the far wall have gone back into the dark. Every time so far. They like dark and damp. That's why they live in walls and under stones. A strong light at the door might send them deeper instead of out.
Might. That's what I've seen, a few times, on a camera. It's not a promise.
Then nobody treats it like one. The light's one thing. The rope, the meter, the three of us and coming back are the rest.
How strong?
Stronger than a helmet.
Work lamps. Eight of them. On a frame, on a pole, so you can stand it in a doorway and stand behind it.
Tomorrow.
You're going.
I'm going.
Then you'll hear my conditions as well as his.
Sarah stays at home. Not the station. Home. Four minutes from my door.
Your wrist is never off. Not for a second. If she calls, you answer. If you don't answer, she calls me, and then I come and find you, and that's worse for you than any centipede.
She means it.
I know she means it.
That's all.
Stand that in a door, and nothing sees past it but you.
Continued where?
That's the thing. There's no next sheet. Not in any revision. It just says continued, and then there isn't anything.
We're not going past the end of that room.
No. You're going to the door, and into the room, and you're going to look. Then you come home.
And Jack. When you get to the end of it. If there's a door, you leave it shut.
I leave it shut.
Say it like you mean it.
I'll leave it shut, Sarah.
Then I can sleep.
I've got all three of you. I've got the bottom pump camera. And I've got the old drawing on the other half of the screen. Turn left at the pump. Follow the edge of the channel downstream.
Copy.
That's farther than it looked on the map.
Everything is.
One bar. The middle one. Rope first.
You first?
I'm the one who promised.
Jack. Stay down. Don't stand up on that. Go across it on your knees. Mark, tell Aiden. It's the middle third. It's wet where the spray comes up.
Tell the others to crawl.
Lamps.
It's going deeper.
I saw it. Nothing else is moving. Aiden, the meter.
Oxygen's low. Lower than out here. Carbon dioxide's high.
Not deadly. But not air I'd want to work in. Not for long.
Then nobody goes in.
It's dead air, lying on the floor. And the floor is where we breathe. So we give it a draft.
Now we wait.
